newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Key facts about Monday's Pakistani elections.
newsitem.headline: Key facts about Monday's Pakistani elections.

text.p: Here are the key facts about Monday's Pakistani elections for a new 217-seat National Assembly (lower house) and four provincial assemblies.
About 56.5 million Pakistanis aged 21 and over are eligible to vote out of a population of more than 131 million.
They will vote at 36,415 polling stations, which are open from 7:00 a.m. (0200 GMT) until 4:00 p.m. (1100 GMT) under the protection of 250,000 troops.
Voting in three constituencies for National Assembly and provincial assembly seats has been postponed because of the deaths of candidates during the election campaign.
Ballot boxes and papers for the National Assembly election are green. Those for provincial assemblies are white.
Officials say 1,758 candidates are vying for seats in the National Assembly and 4,426 for seats in the Punjab, Sindh, North West Frontier and Balochistan provincial assemblies.
Fifty-four parties are contesting the polls, but the main fight is the Pakistan Muslim League (PML) led by Nawaz Sharif and Benazir Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP).
The elections were called by President Farooq Leghari after he sacked Bhutto's three-year-old government on November 5 on disputed charges of corruption and misrule.
Last week the Supreme Court upheld Leghari's action and rejected Bhutto's plea for reinstatement.
The PPP has won two and the PML one of the three party-based elections held since former military ruler General Mohammad Zia-ul-Haq lifted martial law in 1985.
Each party has been allotted a symbol -- an arrow for the PPP and a tiger for the PML -- to help Pakistani voters, two thirds of whom are illiterate, in the polling booths.
Most voters, from the remote valleys of the Hindu Kush in the north to the bullet-scarred slums of Karachi in the south, will simply place a mark by their preferred party's symbol.
The PPP has fielded 161 candidates for the National Assembly and the PML 177.

Ex-cricketer Imran Khan's Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) has put up 132 candidates, a splinter PPP faction led by Bhutto's estranged sister-in-law Ghinwa 66, and the Karachi-based ethnic Mohajir National Movement 55. Others are from smaller parties or are standing as independents.
Non-Moslem minorities who make up about three percent of Pakistan's mainly Moslem population will vote under a separate list for 10 National Assembly seats.
Under Pakistan's first-past-the-post system, the candidate with the highest tally of votes from a constituency is elected.

Candidates may stand simultaneously in more than one constituency for the same assembly or for the National Assembly and a provincial assembly, but may only occupy one seat, forcing by-elections in other constituencies he or she has won.
People in Pakistan's semi-autonomous tribal area bordering Afghanistan are voting for the first time on the basis of universal adult franchise.

They will choose eight National Assembly members, all standing as independents because political parties are not allowed in the area. Previously only tribal elders on government stipends could vote under a restricted franchise.
A record 107 candidates are standing in one tribal constituency in the Kurram Agency area.

Pakistan has closed its border with Afghanistan to prevent Afghans posing as Pakistanis from voting. Many Afghans got Pakistani national identity cards when they lived here as refugees during the long-running conflict in Afghanistan.
